title: The Voices of Jeanne
subtitle: Jeanne d'Arc from Vaucouleurs to Orléans, Reims, Compiègne and Rouen, 1429–1431, and the nullification of 1456
intro: In February 1429 a peasant girl from Domrémy, on the border of Lorraine, persuaded the captain of Vaucouleurs to give her an escort to the Dauphin Charles at Chinon. She said that voices, which she later named as Saint Michael, Saint Catherine and Saint Margaret, had told her to raise the English siege of Orléans and take the Dauphin to Reims to be crowned. Within five months both had happened. Within two years she had been captured at Compiègne, sold to the English, tried by a Church court at Rouen as a heretic and relapsed idolater, and burned in the Old Market on 30 May 1431. Twenty-five years later a papal commission declared that trial null.

Almost nothing in this chapter is a diary in the strict sense, and the form tags say so. Jeanne's own words survive in two ways. Some are letters she dictated (she signed a few, but did not write them herself). Most are her answers at the 1431 trial, taken down by the court's notaries in French, later put into Latin, and turned into English by T. Douglas Murray in 1902. That record was made by her judges, and it is an official record, not a confession of her own choosing. Around it stand dated letters of 1429 from men who saw her or heard about her, a Paris clerk's sketch in the margin of a register, a poem, an Orléans chronicle compiled decades later, the diary of an anonymous Parisian who loathed her, and sworn testimony given at the nullification inquiry by people who had known her 25 or more years before.

The book gives no verdict on the voices. Jeanne said they came from God. Her supporters at Poitiers in 1429 and the nullification judges in 1456 found nothing in her that went against the faith. Her judges at Rouen called her revelations false, and the English regent called her a limb of the Fiend. Modern physicians have offered medical explanations, and these are reported below as dated positions, not diagnoses. The Catholic Church beatified her in 1909 and canonized her on 16 May 1920. These are given as facts of record.

Set side by side, the sources show how one claim travelled. At the centre is the girl who said she heard a voice in her father's garden at thirteen. Around her are an Orléans that ascribed its deliverance to her and a Paris that shut its gates and called her a creature in the form of a woman. A Milanese duke received a letter full of portents, an old poet broke eleven years of silence to praise her, and a bishop recorded every answer she gave. In 1456 her childhood friend, her confessor, her steward and the Bastard of Orléans were asked to remember her under oath.

Warfare runs through every page: the sieges of Orléans, Jargeau and Paris, the battle of Patay, the ransoming and burning. These are told as the sources record them, soberly and without graphic detail.
calendar_note: All dates are in the Julian calendar, as historians of the fifteenth century cite them (the Gregorian reform lay a century and a half ahead); date_iso uses the proleptic Julian date. In much of fifteenth-century France the year began at Easter, so documents written between 1 January and Easter carry the previous year. The Rouen trial record therefore dates its sessions of January–March 1431 to 1430, and modern editions convert them to 1431. Weekdays and feasts (the Sunday of 8 May 1429, the Nativity of the Virgin on 8 September 1429, Ascension week of 1430) are the anchors most sources used.

eyes.name: Jeanne d'Arc (Jehanne, 'la Pucelle')
eyes.role: Peasant girl from Domrémy, about 17 in 1429; leader alongside the Dauphin's captains; prisoner and defendant 1430–31
eyes.where: Vaucouleurs, Chinon, Poitiers, Orléans, Reims, before Paris, Compiègne; prisoner at Beaurevoir and Rouen
eyes.form: dated letters (dictated) and trial answers (official record)
eyes.authenticity: About two dozen letters are known from copies or originals (the Riom letter of 9 November 1429 carries a signature 'Jehanne' believed to be hers). The trial answers survive in the notaries' French minute (partly) and the official Latin record prepared afterwards; both were made by the court that condemned her, and the nullification witnesses later said some passages had been shaped against her. Quotations here follow Murray's 1902 English translation.
eyes.bio: Born in Domrémy around 1412, she said she first heard a voice from God at thirteen. In 1429 she persuaded the Dauphin's court to send her with the relief army to Orléans and then led the march to Reims. She was captured at Compiègne in 1430, tried at Rouen and burned on 30 May 1431. She is the only eye whose words come almost entirely through the record of her enemies.

sources.title: T. Douglas Murray, Jeanne d'Arc, Maid of Orleans, Deliverer of France (1902), Project Gutenberg
Joan of Arc's Letters (Joan of Arc Archive)
Letter to the English, March 1429 (Joan of Arc Archive)

eyes.name: Pierre Cauchon, Bishop of Beauvais
eyes.role: Bishop of Beauvais, member of the English king's council in France; presiding judge of the 1431 trial
eyes.side: Lancastrian (English) France and the University of Paris
eyes.where: Rouen castle and archiepiscopal see, January–June 1431
eyes.form: official record (trial proceedings issued in his name)
eyes.authenticity: The proceedings are notarised minutes issued under Cauchon and the vice-inquisitor Jean Le Maistre; the Latin fair copies were prepared some years later. A short 'posthumous information' dated 7 June 1431, reporting that she recanted her voices before dying, lacks the notaries' signatures, and the notary Guillaume Manchon later refused to vouch for it; its value is disputed.
eyes.bio: A Paris-trained theologian expelled from his see when Beauvais went over to Charles VII in 1429, Cauchon claimed jurisdiction because Jeanne was captured in his diocese. He organised the trial, chose its assessors and sat as judge. The record he presided over is the main source for her own account of her voices.

sources.title: T. Douglas Murray, Jeanne d'Arc (1902): The Trial of Condemnation
History Today: The Trials of Joan of Arc

eyes.name: Journal du siège d'Orléans (anonymous Orléans compiler)
eyes.role: Day-by-day chronicle of the siege of Orléans, October 1428–May 1429, continued to 1429
eyes.authenticity: Survives in a manuscript of the later fifteenth century; it rests on earlier civic notes and borrows from other chronicles (notably the Geste des nobles attributed to Guillaume Cousinot), so it is a later compilation rather than a diary kept during the siege. Edited by Quicherat (1849) and Charpentier and Cuissard (1896).
eyes.bio: The Journal records the siege from the English arrival in October 1428 to the lifting of the siege, in the form of dated entries. It is the city's own account of how a besieged town received the Maid and remembered her within a generation.

sources.title: Journal du siège d'Orléans, ed. Charpentier and Cuissard (1896)

eyes.name: The 'Bourgeois of Paris' (anonymous diarist)
eyes.role: Anonymous Parisian, probably a cleric connected with the University or Notre-Dame
eyes.authenticity: Known from fifteenth-century copies (the author's original is lost); edited by Alexandre Tuetey (1881). The author is unidentified. Some Jeanne entries are written up after the event and repeat the official version from Rouen.
eyes.bio: A Parisian who sided with Burgundy and the English kept a running journal for 44 years of prices, weather, processions and war. He saw the attack on Paris of 8 September 1429 from inside the walls. He wrote of Jeanne with suspicion and contempt, yet reported that many people believed she died a martyr.

sources.title: Journal d'un bourgeois de Paris, 1405–1449, ed. A. Tuetey (1881), Project Gutenberg

eyes.name: Christine de Pizan
eyes.role: Poet and author, about 65, living in retreat in an abbey (generally identified as Poissy, where her daughter was a nun)
eyes.authenticity: The Ditié de Jehanne d'Arc survives in three manuscripts; its closing lines date it to the last day of July 1429. It is the only work about Jeanne written in her lifetime by a known author.
eyes.bio: The most celebrated woman writer of her age had fallen silent after fleeing Paris in 1418. The news of Orléans and Reims drew from her a 61-stanza poem hailing Jeanne as the fulfilment of prophecy and an honour to women. It is probably Christine's last work.

sources.title: Christine de Pizan, Ditié de Jehanne d'Arc, ed. Kennedy and Varty (1977)

eyes.name: Clément de Fauquembergue
eyes.role: Greffier (clerk) of the Parlement of Paris
eyes.authenticity: The original register of the Parlement's council is in the Archives nationales, Paris. The marginal pen drawing of a girl with banner and sword is attributed to him; he never saw her, so it is not a portrait.
eyes.bio: Fauquembergue kept the Parlement's council register. On 10 May 1429 he entered the news from Orléans and, in the margin, drew a figure of the Maid from hearsay, the only image of her made in her lifetime.

sources.title: Register of the Council of the Parlement of Paris (Bridgeman Images record)

eyes.name: Perceval de Boulainvilliers
eyes.role: Councillor and chamberlain of Charles VII, seneschal of Berry
eyes.authenticity: Preserved in a copy in a Milanese / Italian collection and edited by Quicherat (vol. V). Dated 21 June 1429 in the standard editions; one modern summary gives 21 July.
eyes.bio: Writing to Filippo Maria Visconti, Duke of Milan, Boulainvilliers sent the Maid's story to Italy within weeks of Patay. His letter is the source of her traditional birth on the night of Epiphany and of the portents said to have accompanied it. It shows how quickly a court began to tell her story as a wonder.

sources.title: Joan of Arc Archive, footnote on Boulainvilliers' letter

eyes.name: Guy de Laval (later Guy XIV)
eyes.role: Young Breton nobleman, about 23, joining the royal army with his brother André
eyes.authenticity: The original is lost; the text survives in copies and was edited by Quicherat (vol. V, pp. 105–111).
eyes.bio: Guy and André de Laval rode to join the king after Orléans. Guy's letter home to his mother and grandmother at Vitré is the liveliest eyewitness picture of Jeanne in armour. It also records how short of money the court was.

sources.title: Letters from Gui and André de Laval, June 8, 1429 (saintjoandarc.org)

eyes.name: John of Lancaster, Duke of Bedford
eyes.role: Regent of France for his nephew Henry VI
eyes.authenticity: His challenge to Charles VII of August 1429 is preserved in Monstrelet's chronicle. His English memorandum to the king's council, which blames the Pucelle for English reverses, survives in the Privy Council records; it is printed with 1434 and is usually dated 1433–34, though some reprints title it 1429.
eyes.bio: Bedford was the man Jeanne's Letter to the English addressed as 'you who call yourself Regent'. He governed Lancastrian France through the whole of her career. His words show the English view: her success was the work of sorcery, not of God.

sources.title: Letter of the Duke of Bedford calling Joan of Arc a witch (saintjoandarc.org)

eyes.name: Jean, Bastard of Orléans, Count of Dunois
eyes.role: Commander of the defence of Orléans in 1429; in 1456 a senior royal lord
eyes.authenticity: Deposition of 22 February 1456 in the nullification record (ed. Duparc, vol. I). Given 27 years after the events, before a court whose purpose was to clear her.
eyes.bio: Half-brother of the captive Duke of Orléans, Dunois commanded the city when Jeanne arrived and fought beside her to Paris. His testimony is the fullest account by a fellow commander. It includes what she told the king about how her counsel came to her.

sources.title: Joan of Arc Archive, footnote on Dunois' testimony

eyes.name: Jean Pasquerel
eyes.role: Augustinian friar, her confessor and chaplain from Tours in 1429
eyes.where: With her at Tours, Blois and Orléans, 1429
eyes.authenticity: Deposition of 4 May 1456 in the nullification record (ed. Duparc, vol. I). Given 27 years after the events; he was among her closest companions.
eyes.bio: Pasquerel heard her confessions and carried her banner of the Virgin and of Christ through the Orléans campaign. In 1456 he described her piety, her foreknowledge of her wound at the Tourelles, and her last appeals to the English captain Glasdale.

sources.title: Joan of Arc Archive, footnote on Pasquerel's testimony

eyes.name: Jean d'Aulon
eyes.role: Squire assigned as her steward (maître d'hôtel) in 1429; captured with her at Compiègne
eyes.where: With her from Poitiers to Compiègne; testified at Lyon 1456
eyes.authenticity: Deposition taken at Lyon on 28 May 1456 for the nullification court. Given 27 years after the events.
eyes.bio: A veteran soldier given charge of her household, d'Aulon was beside her in most actions from Orléans to her capture, and shared her captivity at first. His long deposition is the most military of the testimonies.

sources.title: Joan of Arc Archive, footnote on d'Aulon's testimony

eyes.name: Hauviette de Sionne
eyes.role: Childhood friend from Domrémy, three or four years younger than Jeanne
eyes.authenticity: Deposition of 29 January 1456 at the Domrémy inquest, answering the court's set articles; given about 27 years after Jeanne left.
eyes.bio: Hauviette grew up with Jeanne, slept at her parents' house and spun with her. Her testimony is the voice of the life Jeanne left behind: churchgoing, alms and work in the fields. It records a departure kept secret even from her closest friend.

sources.title: Joan of Arc Archive, footnote on Hauviette's testimony

eyes.name: Giuseppe d'Orsi and Paola Tinuper
eyes.role: Neurologists at the Universities of Foggia and Bologna
eyes.authenticity: Letter to the editor in Epilepsy & Behavior (2016), reported by Live Science. It offers a hypothesis and states that a firm retrospective diagnosis is impossible.
eyes.bio: Two neurologists who reread the condemnation trial record and proposed a medical explanation for the voices. Their letter belongs to a long line of medical readings going back to the nineteenth century, and other researchers have disputed it. It is included as a dated position, not a finding.

sources.title: Live Science: What really caused the voices in Joan of Arc's head?

entries.headline: The English army under Salisbury arrives before Orléans
entries.digest: The Journal opens with the English host arriving on the south bank of the Loire. Their aim was the bridge and its fortified gatehouse, the Tourelles. Within weeks the earl of Salisbury was mortally wounded by a cannon shot from the town, and the English ringed the city with bastilles. The siege that Jeanne's voices would name as her first task had begun.
entries.source_note: Journal du siège d'Orléans, opening entries (ed. Charpentier and Cuissard 1896); date also in standard chronologies.

entries.headline: She leaves Vaucouleurs for the Dauphin with a small escort
entries.digest: After three interviews with the captain Robert de Baudricourt, she set out for Chinon in men's clothes. With her rode a few companions, among them Jean de Metz and Bertrand de Poulengy. At her trial she said Baudricourt sent her off with a sword, telling her to go and let come what might. She also said her voice had told her to go to France two or three times a week. Some historians place the departure about 13 February.
entries.source_note: Chronology at jeanne-darc.info (22 February); her account at the trial, 22 February 1431 (Murray). Two years between the event and her account.

entries.headline: Letter to the English: 'sent by God, the King of Heaven'
entries.digest: While churchmen at Poitiers examined her, she dictated an ultimatum to the King of England, to Bedford and to the captains before Orléans. They were to give up the keys of the French towns they held to the Maid sent by God. If they made peace they would be spared; if not, she would drive them out of France. The letter opens with 'Jhesus Maria' and closes with the date. It was read back to her at Rouen two years later, when she disputed some of its wording.
entries.quote: King of England; and you, Duke of Bedford, who call yourself Regent
entries.source_note: Letter to the English (Joan of Arc Archive, letters index, dated c. 22 March 1429, Poitiers); text as read at the trial, Thursday 1 March 1431, Murray (1902).

entries.headline: The Maid enters Orléans by torchlight
entries.digest: About eight in the evening she rode in, armed, on a white horse, with her banner carried before her and the Bastard of Orléans at her side. Townspeople crowded to touch her and her horse, as if God himself had come down among them. A torch set her pennon alight and she put out the flame with her own hand. She was lodged with the treasurer Jacques Boucher. The Journal says the people felt comforted, as though the siege were already lifted.
entries.source_note: Journal du siège d'Orléans, entry for 29 April 1429; date confirmed by chronology at jeanne-darc.info.

entries.headline: Saint-Loup falls in the first fight she joins
entries.digest: The Journal records the storming of the English bastille of Saint-Loup, east of the town. Jeanne rode out when the fighting was already under way and stayed until it was taken. It was the first English work to fall, and the town rang its bells. The compiler treats it as the turn of the siege.
entries.source_note: Journal du siège d'Orléans, entry for 4 May 1429; date in chronology at jeanne-darc.info.

entries.headline: Her last summons, shot into the English fort on an arrow
entries.digest: There was no fighting on the feast of the Ascension. She had a short letter written to the English at the Tourelles, telling them in the name of the King of Heaven to go home. Because her heralds had been detained, an archer shot it across tied to an arrow. Her confessor, Pasquerel, later said the English shouted insults back and called her a whore of the Armagnacs, and that she wept and called on God.
entries.source_note: Letter of 5 May 1429 (Joan of Arc Archive, letters index); circumstances from Pasquerel's 1456 deposition, 27 years later.

entries.headline: She is wounded; the Tourelles fall at dusk
entries.digest: The Journal describes an assault on the boulevard and Tourelles lasting from morning to evening. Jeanne was struck by an arrow between shoulder and breast, had the wound dressed and returned to the fight. Toward evening, with her standard at the ditch, the French carried the work. The English commander Glasdale and many of his men drowned when the drawbridge gave way under them. That night the town's bells rang and the Te Deum was sung.
entries.source_note: Journal du siège d'Orléans, entry for 7 May 1429; date confirmed by chronology at jeanne-darc.info.

entries.headline: The English draw up, then march away; Mass in the field
entries.digest: On Sunday morning the English left their remaining bastilles and drew up in battle order before the town. The French formed up opposite them. According to the Journal, Jeanne forbade them to attack on the Lord's day unless they were attacked first, and had Mass said in the field. After about an hour the English withdrew toward Meung and Beaugency. Orléans ever since has marked 8 May as the day of its deliverance.
entries.source_note: Journal du siège d'Orléans, entry for 8 May 1429.

entries.place: Parlement of Paris, Palais de la Cité
entries.headline: Paris clerk logs the news and sketches the Maid
entries.digest: In the council register, Fauquembergue noted reports reaching Paris that the Dauphin's men had broken into the English bastilles before Orléans the previous Sunday. With them, it was said, was a Maid alone with a banner. He added that how this had happened was known only to God. In the margin he drew a small figure of a girl with long hair, a sword and a banner. He had never seen her.
entries.source_note: Register of the council of the Parlement of Paris, Archives nationales (Bridgeman Images record of the page); medieval.eu 'Quills of Clerks'. Date 10 May 1429 as given in standard accounts.

entries.headline: White armour, a plunging black horse, and wine for Paris
entries.digest: Guy de Laval wrote to his mother and grandmother at Vitré after meeting her. She was armed all in white except her head, holding a small axe, and her banner was carried furled by a page. A great black horse plunged at her door until she said to lead it to the cross, and then she mounted and it stood still. She called for wine for him and said she would soon have him drink it in Paris. She had sent his grandmother a little gold ring. He also reported that the court was nearly out of money.
entries.source_note: Letter of Guy and André de Laval, Selles, 8 June 1429 (Quicherat V, 105–111), via saintjoandarc.org.

entries.headline: A courtier tells Milan of portents at her birth
entries.digest: Boulainvilliers wrote to the Duke of Milan that the Maid had been born on the night of the Epiphany. He said the villagers felt a strange joy without knowing why, and the cocks crowed for hours. He told of a race among village girls in which she seemed to fly, and of a voice that sent her home to her mother. He then set out her recent victories from Orléans to Patay and described her as sober, of few words and tireless in arms. The letter turns battle news into a story of signs.
entries.source_note: Letter of Perceval de Boulainvilliers to Filippo Maria Visconti (Quicherat V); 21 June 1429 per Atten (2016, citing Bouguenot); joan-of-arc.org footnote 137 gives 21 July.

entries.headline: On coronation day she writes to Burgundy for peace
entries.digest: Charles was anointed and crowned in Reims cathedral, with Jeanne standing near the altar with her banner. That same day she had a letter written to Philip the Good, Duke of Burgundy. It begged him to make a firm peace with the king and to fight the Saracens instead if he must fight. At Rouen, asked why her standard had been at the coronation rather than other captains' banners, she answered that it had been at the labour and so had a right to be at the honour.
entries.source_note: Letter to the Duke of Burgundy, Reims, 17 July 1429, original in the Lille archives (Joan of Arc Archive); trial answer on the standard, March 1431 (Murray).

entries.headline: An old poet breaks eleven years of silence
entries.digest: Christine dated her Ditié to the last day of July 1429. She says she had spent eleven years weeping in an enclosed abbey and now began to laugh again. She hails a girl of sixteen to whom God gave strength beyond men's. She cites Merlin, the Sibyl and Bede as foretelling her, and calls her an honour to the female sex. She predicts that Jeanne will bring the king into Paris, restore the Church and go on to the Holy Land. Within ten weeks the attack on Paris failed.
entries.source_note: Christine de Pizan, Ditié de Jehanne d'Arc, closing dating stanza (ed. Kennedy and Varty, 1977).

entries.headline: Bedford challenges Charles and scorns his 'disordered' woman
entries.digest: Bedford sent Charles a formal challenge to meet in battle. In it he accused Charles of misleading the simple people with the help of superstitious and reprobate persons, among them a disordered and defamed woman who went about in men's clothing. To the regent she was not a messenger of God. She was a scandal used to deceive.
entries.source_note: Bedford's letter to Charles VII from Montereau, 7 August 1429, preserved in Monstrelet's chronicle; date and wording as commonly cited, not checked against an edition.

entries.headline: Attack on Paris on a holy day; 'a creature in the form of a woman'
entries.digest: The diarist was indignant that the Armagnacs attacked on the feast of the Virgin's Nativity. He wrote that they had with them a creature in the form of a woman, whom they called the Pucelle, and that God alone knew what she was. She stood on the bank of the moat and called on the city to surrender in Jesus's name. A crossbow bolt pierced her leg, and her standard-bearer was hit too. He counted the attackers' dead and wounded with grim satisfaction and accused her of leading men to die on a feast day.
entries.source_note: Journal d'un bourgeois de Paris, entry for September 1429 (ed. Tuetey 1881); date of attack per jeanne-darc.info chronology.

entries.headline: A signed request for gunpowder: 'Jehanne'
entries.digest: Writing to the people of Riom, she reported that Saint-Pierre-le-Moûtier had been taken. She asked them to send gunpowder, saltpetre, sulphur, arrows and crossbows for the coming siege of La Charité-sur-Loire. A secretary wrote the letter, and the signature 'Jehanne' at its foot, in a different hand, is thought to be her own. The supplies were promised but did not arrive in time, and La Charité was not taken.
entries.source_note: Letter to the inhabitants of Riom, Moulins, 9 November 1429 (Joan of Arc Archive page).

entries.headline: Paris hears the Pucelle has been taken at Compiègne
entries.digest: The diarist recorded the news that the Maid had been captured in a sortie from Compiègne by the Burgundians. He wrote that she was taken with several of her captains and handed over to Jean de Luxembourg's men. The news was greeted in Burgundian Paris as a deliverance, and he made no secret that he shared the feeling.
entries.source_note: Journal d'un bourgeois de Paris, 1430 entries (ed. Tuetey); capture date per jeanne-darc.info chronology. The exact day of the entry and its wording are not checked against the edition.

entries.headline: Pierronne, who said God spoke to her, is burned in Paris
entries.digest: The diarist recorded the burning of Pierronne, a Breton woman who had been with the Maid's party. She maintained that God often appeared to her in human form and spoke to her as friend to friend. She also refused to say that Jeanne was anything but good and sent from God. He reported her death as a warning, and it showed what awaited a woman in English hands who claimed such visions.
entries.source_note: Journal d'un bourgeois de Paris, 1430 (ed. Tuetey); the day of the month is as usually cited and not checked against the edition.

entries.date_display: Tuesday 9 January 1431 (1430 in the record's Easter-year style)
entries.headline: Cauchon opens the case against the Maid
entries.digest: The record opens with Cauchon assembling doctors and masters at Rouen to begin proceedings 'in matter of faith' against a woman commonly called the Pucelle. He set out his claim to jurisdiction, since she had been taken in the diocese of Beauvais. He ordered information to be gathered about her life, including enquiries at Domrémy, and appointed the promoter and notaries who would keep the record.
entries.source_note: Trial of Condemnation, preliminary proceedings, 9 January 1431 (Murray 1902); date per jeanne-darc.info chronology.

entries.headline: First public session: the quarrel over the oath
entries.digest: Before more than forty assessors, Cauchon required her to swear to answer truly everything asked of her. She would swear to speak the truth about her parents and what she had done since coming into France. Of the revelations from God she would tell no one, she said, except Charles. After argument she swore on the Gospels with that reservation. The bishop forbade her to try to escape, and she replied that she was free to try.
entries.source_note: Trial of Condemnation, First Public Session, Wednesday 21 February 1431 (Murray 1902).

entries.headline: Voice first heard at thirteen, at noon, in her father's garden
entries.digest: She told the court that the first time she heard the voice she was very much afraid. It came at midday in summer, in her father's garden, from the right, toward the church, and it was usually accompanied by a light. She said it had taught her to behave well and to go to church. Later it told her she must go to France and raise the siege of Orléans, and when she said she was a poor girl who could not ride or fight, it told her to go to Baudricourt at Vaucouleurs.
entries.quote: I was thirteen when I had a Voice from God
entries.source_note: Trial of Condemnation, Second Public Session, Thursday 22 February 1431 (Murray 1902). She described events of about 1425, some six years earlier.

entries.headline: 'If I am not, may God place me there'
entries.digest: Jean Beaupère asked her whether she knew she was in the grace of God. The question was a trap: to say yes would be presumption, and to say no would be to admit guilt. Her answer, recorded by the notaries, avoided both. She added that she would be the saddest creature in the world if she knew she was not in God's grace. She said the voice had woken her that night and told her to answer boldly.
entries.quote: If I am not, may God place me there
entries.source_note: Trial of Condemnation, Third Public Session, Saturday 24 February 1431 (Murray 1902).

entries.headline: She names the voices: Catherine, Margaret, and first Michael
entries.digest: Pressed for names, she said the voices were those of Saint Catherine and Saint Margaret, crowned with fine crowns. She said she had leave from God to name them. The first to come, when she was about thirteen, had been Saint Michael, whom she saw with her own eyes, attended by angels. She would say little of their appearance and refused to describe them in detail. She said she had been as glad to see them as to see the court.
entries.quote: It was Saint Michael: I saw him before my eyes
entries.source_note: Trial of Condemnation, Fourth Public Session, Tuesday 27 February 1431 (Murray 1902).

entries.headline: Letter read back; a seven-year prophecy against the English
entries.digest: The court read her Letter to the English, and she said that a few words had been changed from what she dictated. In the same session she declared that within seven years the English would lose a greater stake than they had lost at Orléans, and that she knew it by revelation. Paris returned to Charles VII in April 1436, about five years later. Believers later counted this a fulfilled prophecy, and sceptics a reasonable forecast of the war.
entries.source_note: Trial of Condemnation, Fifth Public Session, Thursday 1 March 1431 (Murray 1902).

entries.headline: Her voices had warned at Melun that she would be taken
entries.digest: Questioned in her prison, she said that in Easter week of 1430, on the moat at Melun, her voices told her she would be captured before Saint John's Day. They said it must be so and that she should not be dismayed but take it in good part, for God would help her. She said she did not know the day or hour, and that had she known she would not have gone out at Compiègne that day.
entries.source_note: Trial of Condemnation, examinations in prison, March 1431 (Murray 1902); assignment to 10 March as in standard editions, not rechecked.

entries.headline: 'Delivered by a great victory'
entries.digest: She said Saint Catherine had told her she would have help, and that her voices promised she would be delivered by a great victory. She did not know whether this meant release from prison or something else. They told her to take everything peacefully and not to fear her martyrdom, for she would come at last to the kingdom of Paradise. Her friends later read 'deliverance' as her death, and her judges read it as a false promise of escape.
entries.quote: I shall be delivered by a great victory
entries.source_note: Trial of Condemnation, morning session, Wednesday 14 March 1431 (Murray 1902).

entries.headline: Before the crowd and the cart, she abjures
entries.digest: On a platform in the abbey cemetery, the preacher Guillaume Érard denounced her before Cauchon, the vice-inquisitor and Cardinal Beaufort. The executioner and his cart waited nearby. As Cauchon began reading the final sentence, she agreed to submit and put her mark to a short abjuration. Cauchon then read a second sentence condemning her to perpetual imprisonment on the bread of sorrow. She was returned to the English-held castle, not a Church prison. In 1456, witnesses disputed what text she had actually been given to sign.
entries.source_note: Trial of Condemnation, 24 May 1431 (Murray 1902); date per jeanne-darc.info chronology.

entries.headline: The voices reproach her abjuration; she takes back men's clothes
entries.digest: Found again in men's clothes, she told Cauchon and the assessors that she had taken them of her own will. She said that since Thursday, Saint Catherine and Saint Margaret had told her of the great pity of the betrayal she had consented to when she abjured to save her life. Whatever she had revoked, she said, she had done for fear of the fire. The court's clerk wrote in the margin the Latin words responsio mortifera, a fatal answer.
entries.source_note: Trial of Condemnation, Monday 28 May 1431 (Murray 1902); date per jeanne-darc.info chronology.

entries.headline: Declared relapsed and handed to the secular arm
entries.digest: After the assessors had voted on 29 May, Cauchon and the vice-inquisitor read the final sentence in the Old Market. It declared her a relapsed heretic, cut her off from the Church and left her to the secular power. She was burned the same morning. The official record ends there. Other witnesses said decades later that she called on the saints and on Jesus to the end.
entries.source_note: Trial of Condemnation, final sentence, 30 May 1431 (Murray 1902); date per jeanne-darc.info chronology.

entries.headline: A hostile diarist records the burning, and what people said
entries.digest: The diarist summarised the charges as the authorities announced them: men's clothes, false visions, the shedding of Christian blood. He said she was burned at Rouen and that the fire was drawn back so the people could see she was a woman. Then he recorded that many people, both there and elsewhere, said she had been martyred for her true lord. Others said the opposite, and he did not hide which side he was on.
entries.source_note: Journal d'un bourgeois de Paris, 1431 (ed. Tuetey); written up from reports, not seen; wording paraphrased from memory of the edition and not rechecked.

entries.headline: A posthumous 'information' says she disowned her voices
entries.digest: A week after her death, a document under Cauchon's authority collected statements from several clerics who had seen her on her last morning. It said she admitted that her voices had deceived her, since they had promised her deliverance. The trial notaries did not sign it. At the nullification, Manchon said he had refused to sign because he had not been present. Historians treat it as a contested text.
entries.source_note: 'Posthumous information' appended to the Trial of Condemnation (Quicherat I; Murray 1902); exact date as usually cited.

entries.date_display: Wednesday 4 July 1431 (feast of Saint Martin le Bouillant)
entries.headline: Paris hears the Inquisitor's sermon against the Maid
entries.digest: At a general procession the Dominican Inquisitor preached on her life to the people of Paris. He said she had worn men's clothes from childhood and claimed visits from Saints Michael, Catherine and Margaret. He said she was in truth deceived by the devil, and he set her beside Pierronne and other women of her party. The diarist set the sermon down at length and approvingly. It was the official version, delivered from the pulpit five weeks after her death.
entries.source_note: Journal d'un bourgeois de Paris, July 1431 (ed. Tuetey); date by feast day as usually cited.

entries.headline: Bedford blames English losses on 'a limb of the Fiend'
entries.digest: Writing in English to the king's council, Bedford looked back on the war. The run of English success had been broken at Orléans by a great blow from God, as it seemed, caused largely by a disciple and limb of the Fiend called the Pucelle. She had used false enchantments and sorcery. He said she had not only killed many English but taken away the courage of the rest.
entries.quote: a disciple and lyme of the Feende, called the Pucelle
entries.source_note: Bedford's memorandum (Quicherat V, 136–137; Proceedings and Ordinances of the Privy Council, vol. 4, p. 223, 1434), via saintjoandarc.org. Dating 1433–34 is approximate; some reprints title it 1429.

entries.headline: A 'Pucelle' who claimed to be Jeanne is shown to Paris
entries.digest: Nine years after the burning, the diarist recorded that a woman claiming to be Jeanne had been brought to Paris. She was exhibited to the people at the Palais and admitted publicly that she was not the Maid. He also noted that many people had believed Jeanne still alive. The episode shows that rumour of her survival outlived the official record of her death.
entries.source_note: Journal d'un bourgeois de Paris, 1440 (ed. Tuetey); month as usually cited and not rechecked.

entries.headline: The friend who was not told: tears at Jeanne's leaving
entries.digest: Hauviette told the commissioners that she had known Jeanne from childhood, being three or four years younger. Jeanne often went to church and to confession, gave alms, and worked at spinning and in the fields like other girls. She said Jeanne left for France without telling her, and that she wept greatly at the news, for she loved her for her goodness. She knew nothing of voices; to her Jeanne had simply been a good girl of the village.
entries.source_note: Deposition of Hauviette de Sionne, Domrémy inquest, 29 January 1456 (Joan of Arc Archive footnotes 171 and 186; Duparc vol. I). About 27 years after the events.

entries.headline: Dunois remembers the wind, and the voice that said 'go'
entries.digest: Dunois testified that when she reached Orléans in 1429, the contrary wind that kept the supply boats from sailing up the Loire changed at once. From that hour he had good hope of her. He recalled that she had rebuked the captains, saying God's counsel was surer than theirs. Afterwards, at Loches, she told the king that when people doubted her she withdrew to pray. Then she heard a voice calling her daughter of God and telling her to go on, and it would help her. He said she was full of joy as she told it.
entries.source_note: Deposition of the Count of Dunois, 22 February 1456 (Duparc, Procès en nullité I, p. 320; Joan of Arc Archive footnote 280). 27 years after the events.

entries.headline: Her confessor recalls a wound foretold
entries.digest: Pasquerel testified that on the eve of the Tourelles assault she told him to stay close to her the next day. She said she would have much to do, and that blood would flow from her body above her breast. He described her weeping when the English insulted her and her pleas to Glasdale to yield to the King of Heaven. He also described her daily devotion and frequent confession, and her dislike of soldiers' swearing.
entries.source_note: Deposition of Jean Pasquerel, 4 May 1456 (Duparc I, pp. 390–395; Joan of Arc Archive footnotes 286 and 197). 27 years after the events.

entries.headline: Her steward recalls 'fifty thousand' of her own at Saint-Pierre
entries.digest: D'Aulon described the campaigns from Orléans onward. At Saint-Pierre-le-Moûtier in November 1429 he saw her left with only a handful of men and urged her to withdraw. She took off her helmet and said she was not alone, that she had fifty thousand of her people with her. Then she ordered faggots brought to fill the moat, and the town fell. He said he could see no one with her but four or five men. He also told of the sortie at Compiègne where they were taken together.
entries.source_note: Deposition of Jean d'Aulon, Lyon, 28 May 1456 (Joan of Arc Archive footnotes 249, 256, 263). 27 years after the events.

entries.headline: Neurologists propose a hypothesis from the trial record
entries.digest: In a letter to Epilepsy & Behavior, d'Orsi and Tinuper suggested that the voices described in the condemnation record fit a rare inherited form of partial epilepsy with auditory features. They pointed to her reports that bells sometimes accompanied the voices and that they came in sleep. Other researchers objected that her near-daily voices do not match a condition with infrequent seizures. The authors accepted that no certain diagnosis is possible after six centuries. Their letter is one in a long line of medical readings and has not settled the question.
entries.source_note: Live Science, report on d'Orsi and Tinuper's letter in Epilepsy & Behavior (May 2016).

convergences.label: The Letter to the English
convergences.note: Jeanne dictated it as a message from the King of Heaven. Bedford, addressed in it as the man 'who call yourself Regent', answered within months with a challenge calling her a disordered woman. Cauchon's court read it back to her in 1431 as evidence against her.

convergences.label: The Tourelles and her wound
convergences.note: The Journal reports the arrow and the victory. Pasquerel, 27 years later, says she foretold the wound the day before. At her trial Jeanne said Saint Catherine had comforted her when she was wounded. One event appears in three registers: civic chronicle, a confessor's memory, and the defendant's own account.

convergences.label: Orléans delivered
convergences.note: In Orléans it was a Sunday of Mass in the field. Two days later in enemy Paris it became a clerk's note of bastilles lost and a girl with a banner, explained only by 'God knows'. For Dunois in 1456 it was the moment the wind changed.

convergences.label: June 1429: the first letters about her
convergences.note: Two letters two weeks apart. Laval describes what he saw: white armour, a restive horse, a cup of wine. Boulainvilliers, writing to Milan, adds cocks crowing at her birth. Eyewitness detail and wonder-story begin within weeks of each other.

convergences.label: Coronation at Reims
convergences.note: On the day itself Jeanne wrote to Burgundy for peace. Two weeks later Christine turned the coronation into fulfilled prophecy and promised Paris next. Both looked forward to peace, but the war went on.

convergences.label: The attack on Paris
convergences.note: Christine had promised that Jeanne would take Paris. The Bourgeois watched her fail at the Porte Saint-Honoré and called her a creature in the form of a woman. Bedford's 'disordered woman' had become the city's enemy at the gate.

convergences.label: Captured at Compiègne
convergences.note: Jeanne said her voices had warned her at Melun that she would be taken before Saint John's Day. D'Aulon was captured beside her. In Paris the Bourgeois greeted the news with relief.

convergences.label: The burning at Rouen
convergences.note: Cauchon's record ends with the sentence. The Bourgeois, hostile to her, still reported that many called her a martyr. Two days earlier Jeanne had said her saints rebuked her for abjuring. A week later a disputed posthumous document claimed she had disowned them.

convergences.label: The nullification sentence at Rouen
convergences.note: Their depositions, given between January and May 1456, fed the court that declared the 1431 process null for fraud and procedural fault. Each remembered a different Jeanne: the village girl, the commander's prophet, the penitent, the soldier.

ties.note: Defendant and judge through more than fifteen sessions in 1431. She told him he was her judge at his peril; nullification witnesses later reported her final reproach to him.
Her Letter to the English addressed him by name. He held her prisoner at Rouen through the trial.
He received her at Orléans and fought beside her from the siege to the attack on Paris.
Her confessor from Tours onward; he heard her confessions throughout the Orléans campaign.
Her steward from 1429; captured with her at Compiègne.
Childhood friends at Domrémy; Jeanne left without telling her.
He met her at Selles in June 1429 and fought in her campaign; she sent a gold ring to his grandmother.
Christine's poem is the only work about Jeanne by a known author in her lifetime; there is no evidence they met.
Both wrote inside Anglo-Burgundian Paris in 1429, the diarist in the streets and the clerk at the Palais where the false Pucelle was later shown.
Cauchon sat on the Lancastrian council in France, and the English crown paid for the trial; the nullification court stressed this dependence.
The Bastard of Orléans is a principal figure of the Journal's siege, and in 1456 he gave his own sworn version of the same days.
Both wrote from Charles VII's court in Berry in June 1429, one to a family in Brittany and one to a duke in Milan.
The neurologists' hypothesis rests entirely on the record kept under Cauchon, the same text that served the 1431 judges and the 1456 nullification.

threads_out.note: The Hundred Years' War ended at Castillon in 1453, the year Constantinople fell. Pope Callixtus III authorised the nullification trial in June 1455 while organising the crusade to answer the Ottoman advance, which led to the relief of Belgrade in July 1456, the same month the Rouen sentence was declared null.

Revolutionary authorities suspended Orléans' annual 8 May festival of her deliverance in the 1790s. Napoleon Bonaparte authorised its revival in 1803, the first step in her rise as a national symbol of France.

In the First World War both France and its allies used her as a patriotic emblem; a 1918 US Treasury poster invoked her to sell War Savings Stamps. Her canonization in May 1920 came eighteen months after the armistice.
The same pope, Benedict XV, reigned during the Fátima apparitions of 1917 and canonized Jeanne on 16 May 1920. The Church tested both claims of heavenly voices or visions by its own procedures.

vantage_key: 0 = the visionary and her judge; 1 = those who stood beside or against her in person (companions, commanders, the Orléans chronicle, the regent); 2 = officials and diarists in enemy Paris; 3 = courtiers and a poet writing at a distance; 4 = modern investigators reading the record.
